passage:
At the office canteen, Asif's phone buzzed on the table again. A message from the group's coordinator: "Missed Wednesday again? Karma does not forget those who drift." Another, from a member: "Saw you at the mall on Saturday. Who were you with?"

Asif's appetite went.

"Same thing?" Karthik asked, from the next desk.

"They say something bad will come if I skip events. And they seem to know where I go."

Karthik put down the fork. "That sounds like control, not care. You don't have to answer everything."

"I feel guilty."

"Guilt is what it's built to make you feel. Start small. Skip one event and don't explain. And come to my cousin's engagement on Sunday. Outsiders, terrible jokes."

Asif laughed for the first time in days. That evening Asif typed "Can't make Wednesday" and sent it, with no apology.

qa.q: What did the coordinator's message say about karma?
qa.a: It said that karma does not forget those who drift.

qa.q: Why did Asif lose the appetite?
qa.a: The guilt and the sense of being watched, from the karma hint and the question about the mall, left Asif uneasy.

qa.q: What small boundary did Asif set?
qa.a: Asif sent "Can't make Wednesday" without an apology, and planned to spend time with outsiders at Karthik's cousin's engagement.

qa.q: How does Karthik see the messages?
qa.a: Karthik sees them as control, not care, and says Asif does not have to answer everything.

grounding: Members guilt Asif for missing events, hint at karma and watch where Asif goes; a colleague names it as control and helps Asif set a small boundary.

passage:
I'm Darshan, and it took me a while to say this plainly: the group was controlling me.

It never looked like force. When I missed a Sunday for my cousin's wedding, Omkar messaged, "We missed your energy. Hope nothing blocks your progress." When my mother fell ill and I skipped two weeks, someone mentioned that "karma has its own timing." They noticed what I ate at office lunches. They asked who my new friends were.

I felt guilty all the time, as if I were letting down a whole family.

What changed things was small. I told Omkar I would come once a month, not every week. My stomach knotted as I typed it. Then I spent that free Sunday playing football with old friends from work, laughing more than I had in a year.

When I finally stopped going, I sent one polite message. I didn't owe them an apology.

qa.q: Why did Darshan miss a Sunday?
How did Darshan feel as the group noticed and commented on every choice?
qa.a: Darshan felt constantly guilty, as if letting down a whole family, and anxious when setting a limit.

qa.q: What small boundary helped Darshan, and why?
qa.a: Going once a month instead of weekly freed time for outside friends, which showed Darshan how much the group had been controlling things.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Darshan's once-a-month message?
qa.a: Omkar may see it as Darshan drifting from progress, since the group treated missing events as a spiritual failing rather than a normal choice.

grounding: The reflective account shows a group using guilt, hints of karma and watching to control a member, and the member setting small boundaries, spending time with outsiders and leaving without shame.

passage:
Team lead's note, design studio, Friday

Pallavi used to be the first to laugh at our Friday lunch. For two months now she has eaten at her desk. Today she told me why, after I asked if she was all right.

She joined a spiritual group last year. Lately, she said, members call her if she misses an evening session, tell her that bad luck follows people who skip, and ask to see her phone "to protect her from negative influences." She said she feels guilty all the time and ashamed to be complaining.

I did not tell her what to believe. I said that care doesn't usually look like checking someone's phone, and that she can step back without being a bad person.

What I did next: I invited her to lunch with the team, and she came. I also gave her the number of the company's counselling line, and she saved it while we sat together.

Chetan

qa.q: What did the group members ask to see?
qa.a: Pallavi's phone, "to protect her from negative influences."

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when she told the team lead why she ate alone?
qa.a: She felt guilty all the time and ashamed to be complaining about the group.

qa.q: Which of Chetan's steps helped, and why?
qa.a: Inviting Pallavi to lunch with the team gave her time with outsiders, and sharing the counselling line gave her a place to talk freely.

qa.q: How might the group members see Pallavi's lunch with her team?
qa.a: They might frame it as a "negative influence" she should avoid, which is part of how they control her.

grounding: A team lead's note shows a young woman whose group guilts her, hints at punishment and watches her phone, and a colleague helping her keep outside ties and know she can leave.
